Puteoli
pew-TEE-oh-ly
proper noun (place)
Greek Potioloi, a major port on the Bay of Naples in Italy, the chief landing for the Alexandrian grain fleet and the place where Paul first found brethren in Italy.

📖 Biblical Definition

Puteoli was the principal port on the Bay of Naples and the usual landing for the great grain ships from Egypt, where Paul came ashore in Italy and found fellow believers. "And the next day we came to Puteoli: where we found brethren, and were desired to tarry with them seven days: and so we went toward Rome" (Acts 28:13-14). The discovery is striking: before the apostle reached the capital, the gospel had already run ahead of him to this Italian harbor, and a company of brethren welcomed the prisoner and his companions. That they could persuade the centurion to let Paul stay seven days shows the favor God gave His servant even in chains. Puteoli testifies that the church of Christ was already scattered through the empire by ordinary believers — merchants, sailors, travelers — long before any apostle arrived, and that the fellowship of the saints spans every distance. A bound man, shipwrecked and weary, stepped onto Italian soil and was met as a brother by people he had never seen, bound to him by one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Puteoli is a picture of the communion of saints: the family of God receiving its own, refreshing the traveler, and speeding him on his way.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The chief port on the Bay of Naples (Acts 28:13-14) where Paul landed in Italy and found brethren who kept him seven days; a witness that the gospel had run ahead of the apostle and that the communion of saints receives its own.

PUTEOLI, proper noun. A major port on the Bay of Naples, landing place of the Egyptian grain fleet.

Where Paul came ashore in Italy (Acts 28:13).

Where he found brethren and tarried seven days.

A witness that the gospel had already reached Italy before the apostle.

A picture of the communion of saints receiving and refreshing the traveler.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 28:13 — "And from thence we fetched a compass, and came to Rhegium: and after one day the south wind blew, and we came the next day to Puteoli:"

Acts 28:14 — "Where we found brethren, and were desired to tarry with them seven days: and so we went toward Rome."

Eph 4:5 — "One Lord, one faith, one baptism,"

Heb 13:2 — "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Puteoli needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the reality of the communion of saints and the spread of the gospel through ordinary believers, ahead even of the apostles.

expand to see more

Clergy-only misreading. A clericalized view imagines the gospel advancing only by official mission. Puteoli tells otherwise: brethren were already gathered in an Italian port before Paul or any apostle came, the fruit of ordinary believers carrying Christ along the trade routes. The dictionary holds that the Great Commission is fulfilled not only through appointed leaders but through the scattered saints who bear witness wherever providence sends them; the church at Puteoli was such fruit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the communion of saints, that real and tender bond by which believers receive one another as family across every barrier of distance and acquaintance. A chained stranger was welcomed as a brother and kept seven days. The same fellowship still binds the people of God, who entertain strangers, refresh the weary, and speed the traveler on his way for the sake of the one Lord they share.
